notes.title: HTTP Versions — Breadth Flashcards
notes.html:
Two topics that hang off HTTP/1.1's limits and HTTP/2 framing.

HTTP Pipelining

Stage: frame · per request

Pipelining lets a client send several requests on one connection without waiting for responses. RFC 9112 §9.3.2 requires the server to answer in the order received, and a client should not pipeline after a non-idempotent request, so the queue just moves to the server. A slow first response holds everything behind it: in our local run, /fast arrived at 304 ms behind a 300 ms /slow, against 1 ms on its own connection. Broken intermediaries made it unsafe on the public internet, and MDN records it as off by default in browsers. HTTP/1.1's limits owns the capture. Stream IDs replaced it.

Protocol Negotiation: ALPN and Alt-Svc

Stage: frame · per connection

ALPN (RFC 7301) puts the choice inside the TLS handshake: the client offers h2,http/1.1, the server picks one, and no round trip is added. It works over TLS on a known port, so it can't advertise UDP. Alt-Svc (RFC 7838) does: a response says h3=":443"; ma=86400, and the client tries QUIC next time. ma defaults to 24 hours, and clear removes it. The HTTPS DNS record (RFC 9460 §9) gives the same hint before any connection, carrying alpn values. HTTP/3 depends on these, and a short ma is your rollback lever. Cleartext h2c by Upgrade is deprecated (RFC 9113 §3.1).

notes.title: HTTP as a Protocol — Message Anatomy & Statelessness
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics · 📜 RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1 · 📜 RFC 9112 §6: Message Body · MDN: Connection management in HTTP/1.x

TL;DR

An HTTP message is a start line, headers and a body, and on HTTP/1.1 each part ends by a rule, not by a label. Meaning (RFC 9110) stays the same across versions; only the wire format (RFC 9112, 9113, 9114) changes. Every limit in this section comes from how the end of a message is found.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:start lineheaders until a blank linebody length from Content-Length or chunksmessage endsnext message begins

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which RFC owns meaning, and which owns HTTP/1.1 bytes? RFC 9110 owns meaning; RFC 9112 owns the wire.
Three ways a response body can end? Content-Length, the zero-size chunk, or connection close.
Stateless means what? The protocol keeps no state between requests; each one carries what it needs.

The idea

Two machines share one TCP byte stream, and TCP gives no message boundaries. So the first job of any protocol above it is to say where a message ends. HTTP/1.1's answer is text: lines end in CRLF, a blank line ends the headers, and a header states the body's length.

That choice made HTTP debuggable with nc and easy to implement, and it carries a cost that shapes the rest of this section. A receiver must parse from the start to find the end, and two parsers that disagree about the end see different messages. There's also no field saying which request a response answers, so order is the only correlation.

Statelessness is the other half. A server can treat each request alone, so any replica can answer. Sessions live in cookies or tokens that clients resend, and caches can reuse responses, which HTTP caching owns.

The trade: readable, simple framing in exchange for position-based boundaries that every later version had to replace.

How it works

Framing is decided in a fixed order, and that order is where bugs live.

Rule What actually happens
Meaning vs bytes RFC 9110 §6 defines an abstract message; RFC 9112 §2.1 writes it as text. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 write the same message as frames.
Host is required RFC 9112 §3.2: a server MUST answer 400 to an HTTP/1.1 request without it.
Transfer-Encoding wins RFC 9112 §6.3: it overrides Content-Length, and a message with both ought to be treated as an error.
Where the round trips go One per request-response when a connection is reused; the budget owns the 3 RTT cold total.
Who in the middle acts on this A proxy parses every message to forward it, so it can disagree with the backend about the boundary (RFC 9112 §11.2).

Evolution

Lineage:1996 HTTP/1.0 (RFC 1945)1997 HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2068)1999 RFC 26162022 RFC 9110 splits meaning from wire format
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): RFC 9110 is STD 97, RFC 9112 STD 99.
  • Changed in RFC 9110 and 9112 (Jun 2022): semantics moved to one document shared by all three versions, so a version change can't alter what a status code means.
  • What won't change: TCP has no message boundary, so a protocol above it must make one.

On the wire

Captured on 1 Nov 2026 with curl 8.7.1 on 127.0.0.1, against a raw Python 3.15.0 socket server that declares 5 bytes and sends 47:

< Content-Length: 5
* Excess found writing body: excess = 42, size = 5, maxdownload = 5, bytecount = 5
* Closing connection
hello

The client stopped at the declared end and treated the other 42 bytes as junk. What if two parsers pick different ends? A 113-byte message carrying both Content-Length: 39 and Transfer-Encoding: chunked, read by two small parsers in Python:

proxy   (reads Content-Length) leftover: b''
backend (reads chunked)        leftover: b'GET /admin HTTP/1.1...'

The proxy saw one request. The backend saw a second one hiding inside the first, which is request smuggling, and RFC 9112 §11.2 is why §6.3 asks for rejection.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -v shows > and < lines per request; nc shows raw CRLFs for a hand-typed GET.
  • In production: per listener, 400 rate and header-too-large rate; per proxy pair, requests rejected for carrying both length headers.
  • Bounded by: ambiguous framing → reject messages with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding, and normalise at the first proxy.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: HTTP splits into meaning and wire format. RFC 9110 defines methods, status codes and headers for every version. HTTP/1.1 writes those as text, ending headers at a blank line and bodies by Content-Length or chunks. It's stateless, so each request carries its own context and any replica can answer. The text format has a limit: boundaries come from position.

Q · Mechanism — How does a client know a response body has ended? Three ways, in priority order. If Transfer-Encoding: chunked is present, it reads chunks until the zero-size chunk. Otherwise Content-Length gives the count. With neither, a response ends when the server closes the connection, which also means the connection can't be reused, and a truncated body looks complete.

Q · Trade-off — Is statelessness free? No. The server is simpler and replicas interchangeable, but state moves onto the wire and into stores. Each request repeats cookies and tokens, and that repetition is what HPACK had to compress away. Session data moves to a cache or token, with its own failure mode. It's usually a good deal because horizontal scaling comes free.

Compare

Property Semantics HTTP/1.1 wire HTTP/2 and 3 wire When you'd care
Defined in RFC 9110 RFC 9112 RFC 9113, 9114 citing behaviour
Message boundary not its concern parsing rules length-prefixed frames proxy safety
Headers fields text lines compressed fields header limits
Correlation request and response position stream ID concurrency

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Missing Host 400 MUST, HTTP/1.1 spec: RFC 9112 §3.2
Body framing methods 3 chunked, length, close spec: RFC 9112 §6.3
Declared vs sent body 5 vs 47 bytes curl closes the connection measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "HTTP/2 changed what a 404 or a GET means"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a new major version usually means new behaviour.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: all three versions share RFC 9110. Only the bytes that carry a message differ, which is why a proxy can change version per hop.
    ↳ Think instead: semantics first, wire format per hop.
  • "Stateless means no state exists"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the word sounds absolute.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the protocol holds none between requests, but applications do, in cookies, tokens and stores. The connection has state too.
    ↳ Think instead: each request is self-contained; state lives somewhere you chose.
  • Not the same: a header's Content-Length vs bytes on the wire
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: normally they match, so the header reads like a measurement.
    ↳ Difference: it's a claim that parsers obey. Bytes past it are the next message, or junk.
    ↳ Think instead: framing is a contract between two parsers; if they disagree, the attacker chooses.
  • Don't reach for connection close to end a response.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the simplest code path, and it needs no length.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a dropped connection looks like a complete body, and you pay for a new connection each time.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler safe option: send Content-Length when the length is known, chunked otherwise.
  • Shelf life: message anatomy and the RFC 9110 split are durable; header size limits are product defaults, so check them per proxy.

Connections

Path:TCP vs UDPHTTP as a protocolHTTP/1.0 vs 1.1
  • Builds on TCP: a byte stream with no boundaries.
  • Owned elsewhere: methods, status codes and headers own meaning.
  • Contrasts with HTTP/2 framing: length prefix against parsing.
  • Used by HTTP/1.1's limits: no ID means order is the only correlation.

notes.title: HTTP/1.0 vs HTTP/1.1 — Persistence, Host, and Chunked Encoding
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9112 §9: Connection Management · 📜 RFC 9112 §7.1: Chunked Transfer Coding · 📜 RFC 1945: HTTP/1.0 · MDN: Connection management in HTTP/1.x

TL;DR

HTTP/1.1 fixed three HTTP/1.0 costs: a new connection per request, one site per IP address, and a body whose length had to be known up front. Persistence, Host and chunked encoding each remove one, and together they gave us reuse, virtual hosting and streaming on one protocol.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:connectrequest with Hostresponse, chunked if length unknownconnection stays opennext request, no handshakeidle timeout closes it

Recall

Prompt Answer
HTTP/1.1's default for connections? Persistent, unless Connection: close says otherwise.
What did Host make possible? Many sites on one IP address, chosen at the server.
What ends a chunked body? A zero-size chunk, 0\r\n\r\n.

The idea

Under HTTP/1.0, a page of ten images meant ten TCP handshakes and ten cold windows. Every connection ended just as it got fast. HTTP/1.1 made reuse the default, so one warm connection serves many requests.

The request line in HTTP/1.0 sent only the path to an origin server, so a server on one address couldn't know which site was wanted. Host fixed that, and a whole hosting industry fits behind it. TLS later needed the same idea one layer down, which is SNI.

A body's length had to be known first, or the connection had to close to mark the end. Generated pages and streams broke that, and closing cost the connection. Chunked encoding sends sized pieces, so the end is explicit, and the connection survives.

The trade: reuse makes a connection long-lived shared state, so stale connections and idle timeouts become your problem.

How it works

The same two requests on each version: the second request's setup round trip is the difference.

Rule What actually happens
Persistence RFC 9112 §9.3: HTTP/1.1 persists by default; 1.0 only with keep-alive, a value that any 1.0 proxy could mishandle.
Host Required since HTTP/1.1. One address serves many sites, and a missing Host gets 400.
Chunks Size in hex, CRLF, data, CRLF, until size 0 (RFC 9112 §7.1). Trailers can follow.
Where the round trips go Reuse removes setup for every later request, 1 RTT for TCP plus 1 for TLS 1.3 (handshake table).
Who in the middle acts on this Each hop chooses its own: Connection headers are hop-by-hop (RFC 9110 §7.6.1), and a buffering proxy can hold chunks back.

Evolution

Lineage:1996 HTTP/1.0 (RFC 1945, Informational)1997 HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2068)1999 RFC 26162022 RFC 9112
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): HTTP/1.0 survives mostly in simple clients and health checks.
  • Changed in RFC 9112 (Jun 2022): the Host and persistence rules stand, restated apart from semantics in RFC 9110.
  • What won't change: long-lived connections need an owner for idle and retry behaviour.

On the wire

Captured on 1 Nov 2026 with curl 8.7.1 and two URLs, against a stdlib server on 127.0.0.1 that logs each client port (Python 3.15.0):

HTTP/1.0: GET /a from port 56661       num_connects=1
          GET /b from port 56663       num_connects=1
HTTP/1.1: GET /a from port 56664       num_connects=1
          GET /b from port 56664       num_connects=0

One port and num_connects 0 is reuse. The server's /chunk path then sent two lines 50 ms apart, read raw:

Transfer-Encoding: chunked

c\r\n{"t":"the"}\n\r\n
e\r\n{"t":"quick"}\n\r\n
0\r\n\r\n

c is 12 and e is 14, so the sizes are hex. -H 'Host: shop.example' reached the same port and logged Host=shop.example: the address chose the machine and the header chose the site.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -w '%{num_connects}' over two URLs prints 1 then 0 when the connection is reused.
  • In production: per service pair, new connections per second against requests per second; per client, reused-connection failures (a stale connection closed by an idle server).
  • Bounded by: a pooled connection the far side already closed → an idle timeout shorter than the server's (connection pooling) and retries of idempotent requests.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: HTTP/1.1 fixed three things. Persistence reuses one connection and removes setup round trips. Host lets one address serve many sites. Chunked encoding sends a body of unknown length without closing the connection. The cost is that connections become shared long-lived state. There's still only one response at a time on each, which is what HTTP/2 goes after.

Q · Mechanism — Why did chunked encoding need to exist, when closing the connection already marks the end? Close works, but it spends the connection, and it can't tell a complete body from a dropped one. Generated content doesn't know its length up front. Chunks make the end explicit with a zero-size chunk, so reuse survives and truncation is detectable. On HTTP/2 it's gone: DATA frames and END_STREAM do that job.

Q · Trade-off — What does reuse cost you? Connections outlive requests, so someone must own them. If a server closes an idle connection just as a client sends on it, the request fails with no response, and the client can't tell whether it ran. Mitigate with a client idle timeout below the server's and retries for idempotent requests. Keepalives and idle timeouts own the middlebox side.

Compare

Property HTTP/1.0 HTTP/1.1 When you'd care
Connection one per request, by default persistent, by default any repeated caller
Host not required required shared IP, proxies
Unknown-length body close to end chunked streaming
Reused handshakes none every later request long RTT

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Connects for 2 URLs, HTTP/1.0 2 two client ports measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026
Connects for 2 URLs, HTTP/1.1 1 same client port measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026
Chunked terminator 0\r\n\r\n ends the body spec: RFC 9112 §7.1
Setup saved per reuse 2 RTT TCP plus TLS 1.3 derived

Pitfalls

  • "Connection: keep-alive is how HTTP/1.1 reuses connections"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: you still see the header in traffic.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: in HTTP/1.1 persistence is the default, and the header is an HTTP/1.0 holdover. HTTP/2 forbids connection-specific headers altogether.
    ↳ Think instead: 1.1 persists unless told close.
  • "Keep-alive means TCP keepalive"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the same word in two layers.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: HTTP reuse sends new requests on an open connection. TCP keepalive sends empty probes to detect a dead peer.
    ↳ Think instead: reuse saves handshakes; probes detect death.
  • Not the same: Host vs SNI
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both name the site, and they usually match.
    ↳ Difference: SNI is in the TLS handshake, chooses the certificate, and comes first. Host is in the HTTP request and chooses the site after decryption.
    ↳ Think instead: one name per layer, and they can disagree.
  • Don't add Connection: close to silence pool errors.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the stale-connection failures stop right away.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you've turned every request into a handshake, and ports and latency pay for it.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler lasting fix: set a client idle timeout below the server's, and retry idempotent requests.
  • Shelf life: these rules are settled. Idle timeouts belong to products, so check them per proxy.

Connections

Path:HTTP as a protocolHTTP/1.0 vs 1.1HTTP/1.1's limits
  • Builds on HTTP as a protocol: chunked is the second way to end a body.
  • Used by buffering vs streaming proxies: chunks only help if the proxy forwards them.
  • Contrasts with HTTP/2 framing: frames replace chunks.
  • Sized by connection pooling: reuse needs a bound.

notes.title: HTTP/1.1's Limits — One Response at a Time, and the Six-Connection Workaround
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9112 §9.3: Persistence · 📜 RFC 9112 §9.4: Concurrency · 📜 RFC 9113 §5: Streams and Multiplexing · MDN: Connection management in HTTP/1.x · HPBN: HTTP/1.X

TL;DR

An HTTP/1.1 response carries no request ID, so a client can match it to its request only by position. One connection therefore delivers one response at a time, in order. Browsers buy concurrency with about six connections per origin, which makes page load scale with RTT × ceil(requests ÷ 6), and no amount of bandwidth touches that term.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:120 requests queued6 connections, 1 request eachwait 1 RTTnext 6 goa slow response holds its connection20 roundspage done

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why can't two responses interleave on one connection? Nothing on the wire says which request a byte belongs to.
Is six in the RFC? No. RFC 9112 §9.4 sets no maximum; six is browser practice.
What did RFC 2616 say? A single-user client SHOULD NOT keep more than 2 connections.
Round trips for 120 small assets on 6 connections? 20, by ceil(120 ÷ 6), plus setup.
Which layer is this blocking at? HTTP. The TCP form is a separate problem.
Draw by hand: a slow response ahead of a fast one One connection: /slow then /fast, /fast waits. Two connections: /fast returns first.

The idea

Your page needs a slow /orders.json and a logo already in cache. On one HTTP/1.1 connection the logo waits for the JSON, even though the server could send it now. It isn't queued for lack of bytes or CPU. It's queued because the response format has no field that would let it overtake. HTTP as a protocol owns why: a body's end is found by position.

So browsers open more connections. Each one is an independent queue, which works, and each costs a handshake, a TLS session and a cold window. The old limit of two connections gave way to about six, and sites then split assets across hostnames to get six more per name.

On a 200 ms path, 120 assets take four seconds in round trips before bandwidth enters the sum. The fix isn't a faster server: the wait sits between requests.

The trade: six connections buy concurrency and pay six handshakes, six cold windows and six competing congestion controllers, and the wait still grows with request count.

How it works

The same two requests on one connection and on two. Only the framing rule differs from HTTP/2, which tags every frame so the second response can overtake.

Concurrency here costs connections, not protocol work. The arithmetic behind every page-weight argument:

rounds  = ceil(requests ÷ connections)      ← one response per connection per round
wait    = RTT · rounds                      ← 200 ms · ceil(120 ÷ 6) = 200 ms · 20 = 4,000 ms
setup   = 1 RTT TCP + 1 RTT TLS 1.3, once   ← 6 connections open in parallel, so 400 ms wall clock

The cold-request total of 3 RTT is owned by the round-trip budget; here it's only the first round of twenty.

Rule What actually happens
Order is forced RFC 9112 §9.3.2: a server that receives pipelined requests MUST respond in the order received, so pipelining moves the queue and doesn't remove it.
Six is practice RFC 2616 §8.1.4 said 2. RFC 9112 §9.4 only says a client ought to limit connections. MDN and HPBN record six in browsers.
Per origin is the loophole Sharding onto img1., img2. multiplies the cap, and adds DNS lookups and cold windows. It harms HTTP/2, so remove it when you upgrade.
Where the round trips go Into waiting for a free connection: the request has been decided and isn't yet on the wire.
Who in the middle acts on this An edge or proxy can multiplex to the client and speak HTTP/1.1 upstream, holding a pool per backend.

Evolution

Lineage:1997 persistent connections (RFC 2068)1999 limit of 2 (RFC 2616 §8.1.4)2009 SPDY announced2015 HTTP/2 (RFC 7540)2022 RFC 9112, no fixed limit
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the behaviour is permanent, and HTTP/1.1 remains the fallback and much of the internal traffic.
  • Changed in RFC 9112 (Jun 2022): nothing on the wire changed here; the connection rules were restated apart from semantics in RFC 9110.
  • What's next: less browser traffic on it. What won't change: without a tag on each message, responses can't overtake.

On the wire

Captured on 1 Nov 2026 from a threaded http.server on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15.0, raw sockets), where /slow sleeps 300 ms. The client writes both requests to one socket, then repeats with two sockets:

pipelined, one connection:  /slow at 304 ms   /fast at 304 ms
two connections:            /fast at   1 ms   /slow at 306 ms

Two runs agreed within 3 ms. Nothing slowed /fast except its place in line.

Break it: does sending without waiting fix the queue? Run this against any local server with a slow path first:

import socket, time
r = lambda p: f"GET {p} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n".encode()
s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 8080))
t = time.time(); s.sendall(r("/slow") + r("/fast"))      # both leave at once
buf = b""
while buf.count(b"HTTP/1.1 200") < 2: buf += s.recv(4096)
print(round((time.time() - t) * 1000), "ms until the fast response arrived")
# look for: the fast response arrives only after the slow one finishes
# naive belief predicts: /fast arrives in about 1 ms, since it left at once

Run on Python 3.15.0, the wait was 301 ms against 1 ms on its own connection. Pipelining changed when the request left, not when the response could return.

Measure it

  • See it: browser devtools' waterfall, per page, shows a staircase with a "stalled" or queueing phase and http/1.1 in the protocol column; devtools owns reading it.
  • In production: per page, requests × RTT at the client; per service pair, new connections per second against requests per second. Equal rates mean no pooling.
  • Bounded by: a queue behind a slow response → a timeout per request, and a connection pool with a bound (connection pooling), or HTTP/2 between the hops that have concurrency.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: HTTP/1.1 has no ID on a response, so correlation is by position: one connection delivers one response at a time, in order. A slow response blocks what's behind it. Browsers open about six connections per origin, which pays six handshakes and six cold windows, and page load still scales with RTT × ceil(requests ÷ 6). That term is what HTTP/2 deletes.

Q · Mechanism — Why does pipelining not fix this? It lets the client send without waiting, but RFC 9112 §9.3.2 makes the server answer in the order received. A slow first response still holds everything behind it: only the queue's location moved, from client to server. That's why the fix needed stream IDs rather than a smarter queue.

Q · Trade-off — If six connections help, why not sixty? Because the cost curve turns. Each connection adds a handshake, a TLS session, a socket on both ends and a cold window, and every one is an independent congestion controller competing at the same bottleneck, unaware of the others. More connections help only while serialisation is the bottleneck; once the network is, they add loss and little throughput. HTTP/2's one warm connection replaces that fight.

Q · Failure — A service calls another at 500 requests per second and gets EADDRNOTAVAIL. What ran out? Ephemeral ports. Without reuse, request rate becomes connection rate, and each close holds a port in TIME_WAIT. Sockets and ports owns the ceiling, about 470 per second to one destination on Linux defaults. The upstream looks healthy because it never saw the requests. Confirm with TIME_WAIT counts and new connections per second at the client. Fix it with a pool, sized by concurrency.

Q · Design — You inherit a page of 120 assets over HTTP/1.1 at 200 ms RTT. What do you do? The binding constraint is four seconds of round trips, so it's a concurrency problem, not a bandwidth one. Terminate HTTP/2 at an edge near the user: that removes the rounds and shrinks RTT. Then unwind sharding, or the upgrade will disappoint. Keep pooled connections to the origin. Watch connections per page and the share of requests on h2. Service communication patterns covers the same call between services; when each version matters owns the per-hop choice.

Compare

Approach In flight per connection Who blocks Cost When you'd pick it
One persistent connection 1 everything behind a slow response none extra one request at a time
Pipelining several sent, 1 answered the server's queue broken intermediaries not on the public internet
Six connections 1 that connection's queue 6 handshakes, 6 cold windows HTTP/1.1 clients
Sharding 1 that connection's queue the above, plus DNS nowhere new; remove it

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Responses at once per connection 1 order preserved spec: RFC 9112 §9.3.2
Connection limit in the RFC none "ought to limit" spec: RFC 9112 §9.4
Older limit 2 single-user client spec: RFC 2616 §8.1.4, obsolete
Browser practice 6 per origin not a standard default (as of Nov 2026): MDN
120 assets, 6 connections, 200 ms 4,000 ms round trips only derived
Same 2 requests, one vs two connections /fast at 304 ms vs 1 ms /slow sleeps 300 ms measured: Python 3.15.0, 1 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "Six connections is in the HTTP spec"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every browser does it, and it behaves like a protocol constant.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: RFC 2616 said 2, and RFC 9112 §9.4 names no number at all. Six came from browser practice, per origin, which is why sharding worked.
    ↳ Think instead: a client policy, not a protocol rule. Servers and proxies set their own limits.
  • "More bandwidth will fix the load time"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: slow pages feel like a thin pipe, and upgrades are sold in megabits.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the wait is in rounds of request and response. On 120 small assets the connections sit idle most of the time, waiting for a turn.
    ↳ Think instead: count rounds and multiply by RTT; check the latency vs bandwidth split.
  • Not the same: HTTP/1.1 blocking vs TCP head-of-line blocking
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are called head-of-line blocking, and both look like a stall.
    ↳ Difference: this one is at HTTP, needs no loss, and comes from order of responses. TCP's needs a lost packet.
    ↳ Think instead: name the layer every time. Different causes, different fixes.
  • Don't carry sharding and sprites into HTTP/2.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: they're established performance advice, and removing them feels like a regression.
    ↳ What goes wrong: sharding splits one multiplexed connection into several, so you measure little gain and blame the protocol. MDN calls it detrimental on HTTP/2.
    ↳ Do instead: treat them as workarounds with an expiry date, and remove them in the same change.
  • Don't reach for HTTP/2 when one request at a time is all you do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: newer sounds strictly better.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a cron job or webhook receiver has no concurrency to multiplex, so you add tooling cost for nothing, and lose reading the wire with nc.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: HTTP/1.1 with connection reuse.
  • Shelf life: the framing rule is permanent. The six is browser policy, so re-check it before quoting it as current.

Connections

Path:HTTP/1.0 vs 1.1HTTP/1.1's limitsHTTP/2 framingHTTP/2's remaining flaw
  • Builds on HTTP as a protocol: positional framing is the cause.
  • Owned elsewhere: sockets and ports owns the port ceiling; the round-trip budget owns cold-request arithmetic.
  • Bounded by connection pooling: the server-side fix, sized by concurrency.
  • Contrasts with HTTP/2: stream IDs delete the division by six.
  • Composes with head-of-line blocking in four places: the same shape elsewhere.
  • Decided in when each version matters: which hop deserves the upgrade.

notes.title: HTTP/2 — Binary Framing, Streams & Multiplexing
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9113 §4: HTTP Frames · 📜 RFC 9113 §5: Streams and Multiplexing · 📜 RFC 9113 §6: Frame Definitions · nginx: HTTP/2 module · HPBN: HTTP/2

TL;DR

HTTP/2 keeps HTTP's meaning and replaces the wire: every message becomes length-prefixed frames, and each frame names its stream. So responses can interleave and overtake on one connection. The trade is that one connection is now one failure domain, and one placement decision for a load balancer.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:TLS picks h2preface + SETTINGSHEADERS on streams 1, 3DATA frames interleavestream 3 finishes firstEND_STREAM closes eachconnection stays open

Recall

Prompt Answer
Frame header size and its two key fields? 9 octets; Length and Stream Identifier.
Which stream IDs does a client use? Odd; server-initiated even; 0 is the connection; never reused.
Default limit on concurrent streams? None until advertised; RFC 9113 recommends no smaller than 100.
Default flow-control window? 65,535 octets, per stream and per connection.
Round trips does choosing h2 add? None: ALPN rides the TLS handshake.
Draw by hand: two requests, second answer first HEADERS 1, HEADERS 3, then DATA 3 ahead of DATA 1, each tagged.

The idea

A page asks for a slow API result and a small script. On HTTP/1.1 the second waits or needs another connection, because a response has no identity. HTTP/2 fixes that one thing: it cuts every message into frames, and each frame carries a stream number.

Now the server can send the script at once, send half of the API result, and finish later. Multiplexing isn't a feature on top of the framing: it is the framing. So the six connections collapse into one, with one handshake and one window that stays warm. Semantics don't move: RFC 9110 is shared by all versions.

"Binary" isn't why it's fast. Parsing was never the bottleneck. The length prefix removes delimiter scanning, and the stream ID removes the ordering rule.

The trade: you delete the wait per request and pay with a single failure domain, a connection that L4 balancers can't split, and a wire you can't read by eye.

How it works

Every frame starts with the same nine octets.

+-----------------------------------------------+
|                 Length (24)                   |
+---------------+---------------+---------------+
|   Type (8)    |   Flags (8)   |
+-+-------------+---------------+-------------------------------+
|R|                 Stream Identifier (31)                      |
+=+=============================================================+
|                   Frame Payload (0...)                      ...
+---------------------------------------------------------------+

RFC 9113 §4.1 lists these fields as a field list; the art is RFC 7540's drawing of the same layout. Length excludes the header, so no scanning. Stream Identifier is what permits interleaving.

The exchange below follows the capture in : the second request overtakes the first.

Stream 3 was asked second and finished first, which HTTP/1.1 can't express.

Rule What actually happens
Streams A client opens odd IDs, each higher than the last. IDs can't be reused, so a client that runs out opens a new connection and a server can force it with GOAWAY (§5.1.1).
Flow control WINDOW_UPDATE credits apply per stream and per connection, and only to DATA (§5.2). Without them one download could starve the rest.
Cancellation RST_STREAM ends one stream and leaves the connection alone. On HTTP/1.1, cancelling usually meant closing the connection.
Where the round trips go Setup is the same as TLS over TCP; the preface rides with it. After that, every request leaves at once, so request count stops multiplying RTT.
Who in the middle acts on this Only an L7 proxy reads streams. An L4 balancer places the whole connection, so a long-lived connection pins to one backend.

Evolution

Lineage:2009 SPDY announced2012 first HTTP/2 draft2015 RFC 75402022 RFC 9113 obsoletes 7540 and 8740
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the default for browsers and every major proxy; gRPC depends on it.
  • Changed in RFC 9113 (Jun 2022): the 7540 priority scheme and the h2c Upgrade path are deprecated, Host and :authority may no longer disagree, and TLS 1.3 use is folded in. Cleartext use now means prior knowledge.
  • What's next: implementations keep adding stream-abuse limits. What won't change: one TCP connection means one shared stall.

On the wire

Captured on 1 Nov 2026: curl 8.7.1 (--http2 -Z, two URLs) against a 64-line stdlib HTTP/2 server on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15.0, TLS 1.3, ALPN h2) that logs each frame. /slow was requested first:

recv SETTINGS      stream=0 len=18  # 0x3=100, 0x4=10485760, 0x2=0
recv WINDOW_UPDATE stream=0 len=4   # curl opens the connection window
recv HEADERS       stream=1 len=35  # ② /slow, full header block
recv HEADERS       stream=3 len=11  # ③ /fast, mostly table references
send HEADERS       stream=3 len=1   # ④ overtakes stream 1
send DATA          stream=3 len=7
send HEADERS       stream=1 len=1   # ⑤
send DATA          stream=1 len=7
send DATA          stream=3 len=7   # interleaved with stream 1
send DATA          stream=3 len=7 flags=0x1  # ⑥ END_STREAM
send DATA          stream=1 len=7 flags=0x1  # ⑦ END_STREAM

curl reported /fast done at 106 ms and /slow at 162 ms. 0x2=0 is SETTINGS_ENABLE_PUSH off: this client refuses push.

Break it: is response order still tied to request order? This server deliberately answers the later stream first:

def mux(send, a, b):                       # a was requested first
    send(HEADERS, END_HEADERS, b, status_200); send(DATA, 0, b, b"fast-1\n")
    time.sleep(.05)
    send(HEADERS, END_HEADERS, a, status_200); send(DATA, 0, a, b"slow-1\n")
    send(DATA, 0, b, b"fast-2\n"); send(DATA, END_STREAM, b, b"fast-3\n")
    time.sleep(.05); send(DATA, END_STREAM, a, b"slow-2\n")
# look for: the second URL completing first, with both bodies intact
# naive belief predicts: a client error, or one body containing the other's bytes

Run with curl 8.7.1: /fast finished about 55 ms before /slow, and both bodies were complete. Against an HTTP/1.1 parser those bytes would be nonsense, because nothing would say whose they are.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -w '%{http_version} %{num_connects}' shows 2 and one connect for many URLs; openssl s_client -alpn h2 prints ALPN protocol: h2, which it did here on 1 Nov 2026.
  • In production: per connection, active streams and RST_STREAM rate; per backend, requests per second. Skew across backends with flat errors means connections have pinned.
  • Bounded by: a client opening or resetting streams faster than you can handle → SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS, a request rate limit per connection, a connection age limit.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: HTTP/2 keeps the semantics and changes the wire to length-prefixed frames, each tagged with a stream ID. Frames from many requests can interleave on one connection, so a slow response no longer blocks a fast one, and the six connections collapse into one. Header compression is a separate win. What it doesn't change is TCP underneath, so one lost packet still stalls every stream.

Q · Mechanism — Why does HTTP/2 need its own flow control if TCP has one? TCP's window protects the receiver of the connection as a whole. Multiplexing creates a new problem inside it: one large download could fill the shared buffers and starve small responses. So HTTP/2 credits DATA per stream and per connection with WINDOW_UPDATE. The default 65,535 octets is small for a long fat path, which is why clients raise it; curl advertised 10 MiB here. TCP flow control owns the lower window.

Q · Trade-off — One connection instead of six: what did you give up? Isolation and balancing. Six connections meant a loss stalled a sixth of the work; one means all of it. An L4 balancer that spread connections now places a hundred requests at once, so new backends sit idle until something reconnects. On a normal path HTTP/2 still wins clearly. Between low-concurrency callers, the win is small, and HTTP/1.1 stays easier to read.

Q · Failure — An edge tier's memory climbs, while connections and request rate look flat. What's running out? Per-stream state: concurrent streams, each with buffers and a window, on top of a per-connection header table. The connection dashboard hides it, and an attacker can drive it: the 2023 Rapid Reset attack (CVE-2023-44487) opened and reset streams in a loop, so cancelled streams stopped counting against the limit. Confirm with active streams and RST_STREAM rate per connection. Cap streams, count resets, and close abusive connections.

Q · Design — Design the edge for browsers and gRPC services on one platform. Where does HTTP/2 sit? The binding constraint is that multiplexing defeats connection-level balancing, so the protocol and balancer layer are one decision. Terminate HTTP/2 at an L7 edge, which can place each stream. Use pooled HTTP/2 to backends, and set a maximum connection age so scale-outs take traffic. Watch request skew across backends first. gRPC on HTTP/2 owns the mapping, and service communication patterns where the call is chosen.

Compare

Frame Type What it does When you'd see it
DATA 0x0 body bytes, flow controlled every response
HEADERS 0x1 compressed headers, or trailers with END_STREAM every request
SETTINGS 0x4 per-connection parameters, acknowledged connection start
RST_STREAM 0x3 cancels one stream abort, deadline
GOAWAY 0x7 graceful close, last stream processed drain, deploy
WINDOW_UPDATE 0x8 flow-control credit long downloads

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Frame header 9 octets 24 + 8 + 8 + 1 + 31 bits spec: RFC 9113 §4.1
Max frame default 16,384 octets raise with SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE spec: RFC 9113 §4.2
Initial window 65,535 octets stream and connection spec: RFC 9113 §6.5.2
Concurrent streams no limit initially "no smaller than 100" advised spec: RFC 9113 §5.1.2, §6.5.2
Connections per origin 1 SHOULD NOT open more spec: RFC 9113 §9.1
nginx stream limit 128 http2_max_concurrent_streams default (as of Nov 2026): nginx
ALB requests in parallel 128 per connection HTTPS listeners default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB listeners

Pitfalls

  • "HTTP/2 is faster because binary parses faster"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: binary sounds efficient, and it's the first word in every summary.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: parsing wasn't the wait. Round trips between requests were, and frames remove those. Header size is HPACK's separate job.
    ↳ Think instead: stream IDs are the point; binary only makes them cheap to carry.
  • "HTTP/2 changed HTTP"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a new major number suggests new behaviour.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: methods, codes and caching stay in RFC 9110. A proxy can take HTTP/2 from a client and speak HTTP/1.1 upstream.
    ↳ Think instead: same message, different envelope format per hop. Version is a hop's property.
  • Not the same: a stream vs a connection
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: on HTTP/1.1 they behaved the same, one exchange at a time.
    ↳ Difference: streams are cheap and short, and belong to one request. The connection is long-lived and is what a balancer sees and TCP stalls.
    ↳ Think instead: balance and limit streams; budget and recycle connections.
  • Don't leave stream limits at a default you haven't read.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: RFC defaults look safe, and traffic works.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the initial limit is none. CONTINUATION floods (VU#421644, Apr 2024) and Rapid Reset showed limits on streams alone are not enough.
    ↳ Do instead: advertise a limit, cap headers, and rate-limit resets per connection.
  • Don't put multiplexed traffic behind an L4 balancer and call it balanced.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the balancer's health checks pass, and it worked for HTTP/1.1.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every stream on a connection lands on one backend, and new pods stay idle with no error.
    ↳ Do instead: use L7 balancing or a maximum connection age; for one-at-a-time callers, the simpler HTTP/1.1 pool is fine.
  • Shelf life: framing is durable. Stream defaults, abuse limits and proxy behaviour move, and the chapter map dates them.

Connections

Path:HTTP/1.1's limitsHTTP/2 framingHPACK, priorities, pushHTTP/2's remaining flaw
  • Builds on HTTP/1.1's limits: frames remove positional correlation.
  • Owned elsewhere: ALPN card owns version selection; gRPC and HTTP/2 balancing owns pinned connections.
  • Bounded by the timeout hierarchy: stream limits stop abuse, and timeouts stop waiting.
  • Used by gRPC on HTTP/2: one RPC is one stream.
  • Evolved into HTTP/3: the transport absorbs streams.
  • Decided in service communication patterns: protocol per service boundary.

notes.title: HPACK, Stream Priorities & Server Push
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 7541: HPACK · 📜 RFC 9218: Extensible Prioritization · 📜 RFC 9113 §8.4: Server Push · Chrome: Removing HTTP/2 Server Push

TL;DR

HTTP/2 shipped three additions on top of framing. HPACK survived, priorities were replaced, and push was switched off by clients. HPACK replaces repeated headers with table references, per connection; RFC 9218's simple u and i replaced the priority tree; 103 Early Hints took over what push tried to do.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:first request sends literalsboth ends add them to a tablenext request sends indexesheader block shrinksPriority: u=1 advises orderserver schedules

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why not gzip headers? CRIME: compressed size leaks secrets. HPACK compresses without shared-window matching.
What happens to an entry larger than the table? The table empties, and nothing is added.
Who disabled push, and when? Chrome 106 in Sep 2022, Firefox 132 in Oct 2024.

The idea

Every request on a connection repeats the same cookie, user agent and accept headers. On a page of many requests, that's the same bytes uploaded again and again, on a path where upload windows start small. Compress them? Gzip over headers leaked secrets through CRIME, so HPACK takes a different route: a shared table of whole fields, and an index instead of a repeat.

Priorities tried to tell the server what to send first, using a dependency tree. Few did it well. Push tried to send assets before they were asked for, without knowing what the client had cached, so it often wasted bytes. Neither survived real clients.

The trade: a per-connection table that saves bytes and, as a price, must stay in sync, which forces in-order header decoding.

How it works

The dynamic table only works if both ends make the same changes in the same order.

Rule What actually happens
Static table 61 fixed entries; index 2 is :method GET, and 8 is :status 200 (RFC 7541).
Dynamic table Starts at 62, evicts oldest first. Each entry costs name + value + 32. Default size is 4,096 octets.
Never indexed A sensitive field can be marked so no intermediary adds it to a table (RFC 7541 §6.2.3).
Where the round trips go Not into HPACK: it saves bytes, so it helps only when small upload windows would otherwise force an extra trip.
Who in the middle acts on this Each hop has its own table. A proxy decodes and re-encodes, so priorities and compression don't pass end to end.

Evolution

Lineage:2012 CRIME2015 HPACK (RFC 7541)2017 103 Early Hints (RFC 8297, Experimental)2022 priorities (RFC 9218) and Chrome off push2024 Firefox off push
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026) for HPACK. RFC 9113 §5.3.2 deprecates the old priority tree. Push isn't formally deprecated: RFC 9113 §8.4 says only that it's difficult to use effectively.
  • Changed in Chrome 106 (Sep 2022) and Firefox 132 (Oct 2024): push disabled by default. Chrome reported use falling from 1.25% to 0.7% of HTTP/2 sites. Safari has published no notice that we found, though Mozilla's Sep 2024 test saw it reject push streams.
  • What's next: nginx made http2_push obsolete in 1.25.1 and points to early_hints. AWS ALB doesn't support push.
  • What won't change: a table has to stay in sync, so QPACK exists.

On the wire

Captured on 1 Nov 2026: curl 8.7.1 sends one request three times on one connection, against a stdlib HTTP/2 server on 127.0.0.1 that logs each HEADERS frame (Python 3.15.0):

Cookie in the request                     1st request  2nd  3rd
400 random base64 characters                365 bytes   10   10
400 copies of "a"                           293 bytes   10    -
5,000 characters, over the 4,096 table     4081 bytes 4057 4057

second block starts: 82 87 c1 04 0...
  82 :method GET  87 :scheme https  c1 dynamic reference  04 literal path

The cookie cost hundreds of bytes the first time and about one byte after that. The third row is the surprise: a field larger than the table is never indexed, so a large cookie gets no benefit at all.

Measure it

  • See it: nghttp -v on a machine that has it decodes each header block (illustrative here); a frame logger shows HEADERS lengths falling as above.
  • In production: per connection, header bytes against body bytes on upload; per listener, 431 rate and header-table memory.
  • Bounded by: a dynamic table per connection → SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE and a maximum header list size, which stop one client inflating memory.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: HPACK makes headers small by sending an index into a table both ends maintain, so a repeated cookie costs a byte. Priorities were a tree that few implemented, and RFC 9218 replaced them with u for urgency and i for incremental. Push guessed what clients needed without knowing their cache, so Chrome turned it off in 2022, Firefox in 2024.

Q · Mechanism — Why did HPACK avoid general compression? CRIME showed that when an attacker can add text next to a secret, compressed size reveals whether they matched. HPACK only matches whole fields against a table, and encodes the rest with a fixed Huffman code, so a guess has to match an entire value. RFC 7541 §7.1 adds never-indexed fields for short secrets, so a guess can't be tested at all.

Q · Trade-off — Why did push fail, when sending early seems so clearly useful? Because the server doesn't know the client's cache. Pushing a stylesheet the browser already has wastes bytes on the slowest part of the path, and the client's cancellation arrives a round trip late. Measured gains were rare, so usage fell. 103 Early Hints inverts it: the server suggests, and the client decides using its cache, at the cost of one more response head.

Compare

Mechanism Status, Nov 2026 Replaced by When you'd use it
HPACK in use QPACK on HTTP/3 always on HTTP/2
RFC 7540 priority tree deprecated by RFC 9113 RFC 9218 never in new work
RFC 9218 Priority in use, advisory none ordering page resources
Server push off in Chrome, Firefox 103 Early Hints not for browsers

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Static table entries 61 fixed, in the RFC spec: RFC 7541
Default table size 4,096 octets SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE spec: RFC 9113 §6.5.2
Entry overhead 32 octets name + value + 32 spec: RFC 7541
u urgency 0–7, default 3 lower is sooner spec: RFC 9218
400-char cookie, then repeat 365 → 10 bytes HEADERS frame measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026
5,000-char cookie, then repeat 4081 → 4057 bytes over the table measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "HPACK makes headers free"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: repeated headers shrink to a byte in a demo.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the table is per connection, starts empty, and has 4,096 octets by default. A field larger than that is never indexed, as the capture shows.
    ↳ Think instead: header size still matters; keep cookies small.
  • "RFC 9113 deprecated server push"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every browser dropped it, and it sounds official.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: §8.4 says only "difficult to use effectively". Clients ended it, by default settings, and SETTINGS_ENABLE_PUSH=0 tells a server so.
    ↳ Think instead: deployed status differs from spec status; quote them apart.
  • Not the same: push vs Early Hints
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both try to get a resource moving before the page asks.
    ↳ Difference: push sends bytes unasked. 103 sends only a hint, and the client fetches what it lacks.
    ↳ Think instead: server guesses vs client decides.
  • Don't build a new feature on HTTP/2 push.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's in the RFC, and some servers still accept the config.
    ↳ What goes wrong: browsers refuse the streams, so you maintain a code path nothing uses.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: a Link: rel=preload header, or 103 Early Hints where your edge supports it.
  • Shelf life: HPACK is stable. Priorities and Early Hints support differ by product, so check them before relying on them.

Connections

Path:HTTP/2 framingHPACK, priorities, pushHTTP/2's remaining flaw
  • Builds on HTTP/2 framing: HEADERS frames carry HPACK blocks.
  • Evolved into QPACK: the same table without forced ordering.
  • Composes with headers: what's worth compressing.
  • Contrasts with server-sent events: the kind of server-to-client delivery that does work.

notes.title: HTTP/2's Remaining Flaw — TCP Still Stalls Every Stream
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9113 §9.1: Connection Management · HPBN: HTTP/2 · Langley et al., SIGCOMM 2017: The QUIC Transport Protocol

TL;DR

HTTP/2 removed blocking at HTTP and left it at TCP, and it then raised the stakes by moving everything onto one connection. One lost packet used to stall a sixth of the work; now it stalls all of it. The mechanism belongs to TCP head-of-line blocking; this note covers how much blast radius grew and how to tell whether you have the problem.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper packet
Flow:many streams, one TCP connectionone packet lostlater bytes wait in the kernelevery stream stallsretransmit arrivesall resume together

Recall

Prompt Answer
What decides how many streams one loss stalls? All streams on that connection, because TCP sees one byte stream.
Which metric shows it? A tail that tracks retransmits by network cohort, with a clean median.
Is it worse than HTTP/1.1 under loss? It can be: one connection against six means a larger blast radius.

The idea

Stream 3 has all its bytes sitting in a receive buffer, and the application can't read them, because a packet from stream 1 went missing ahead of them. TCP promised ordered bytes, and it knows nothing about streams. That note owns the mechanism; don't look for a fix inside HTTP/2, because the frames that would need releasing are below it.

What HTTP/2 changed is the scope. Six connections split a loss across six independent recoveries, so a stall hit a sixth of the work. One connection puts every request behind it, and RFC 9113 §9.1 tells clients to stay on one. So under loss, the multiplexing win is partly returned. HPBN lists this as a known downside.

It's still usually a good deal: the wait HTTP/2 removes happens on every page, and this stall only on loss. Those stalls land in the tail, so averages hide them.

The trade: one warm, efficient connection, paid for with one shared failure.

How it works

The same missing packet at the same offset, with different scope.

Exposure is simple arithmetic. How long each stall lasts depends on how the loss is found.

stalls per page   = packets · loss rate            ← 300 packets · 1% = 3
streams per stall = all on the connection (HTTP/2), 1 (HTTP/1.1, QUIC)
stall length      = about 1 RTT by duplicate ACKs, at least 1 RTO by timeout

Sequence numbers and retransmission owns RTO, whose Linux floor is 200 ms; 1 s is the initial value, before any sample. Short or sparse responses may not produce enough duplicate ACKs, so they're the ones that fall to the timeout, which is why token streams feel this most.

Rule What actually happens
Scope Every stream on the connection waits, including those with all their bytes present.
Who can't help HTTP/2 flow control and priorities act above TCP, and neither can release bytes the kernel holds.
Where the round trips go Each loss adds at least one RTT to everything on the connection. Setup is unaffected.
Who in the middle acts on this An edge ends the lossy last mile, so a stall hurts the client's connection and not the backbone's.

Evolution

Lineage:2015 HTTP/2 moves all streams onto one connection2017 Google reports QUIC results2021 QUIC (RFC 9000)2022 HTTP/3 (RFC 9114)
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): well understood, and permanent over TCP.
  • Changed in RFC 9113 (Jun 2022): nothing here. The flaw is structural, and §9.1's advice of one connection stands.
  • What won't change: while TCP presents one ordered byte stream, streams on top share its stalls.

On the wire

Real loss needs a shaped link, so this stands in for it: a stdlib relay on 127.0.0.1 holds any chunk containing LOST for 300 ms, as a gap would. tcpdump isn't available here, and nothing was dropped. Captured on 1 Nov 2026 with curl 8.7.1 and Python 3.15.0:

                      /a (held)   /b (small, unrelated)
HTTP/2, 1 connection   0.304 s      0.304 s
HTTP/1.1, 2 connections 0.305 s     0.001 s

Three runs each gave 0.302–0.305 s and 0.001–0.003 s for /b, respectively. The server sent /b at once, and on the shared connection it still waited for /a. The bytes /b needed existed, held behind someone else's.

Measure it

  • See it: nstat -az TcpRetransSegs before and after, on Linux, illustrative here; a tail that rises with retransmits while p50 stays flat.
  • In production: per cohort (network type, ASN), p99 and p50 by negotiated version; retransmit rate at the edge; stall gaps between chunks per stream.
  • Bounded by: a lossy last mile → a retry budget and deadlines that outlast one RTO, and HTTP/3 where measured.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: HTTP/2 fixed blocking at HTTP, but TCP still delivers one ordered byte stream, so one lost packet stalls every stream on the connection. Worse, a stall used to touch one of six connections and now touches all the work. It shows up in a lossy cohort's tail, not the median. Fixing it needs a transport that knows about streams, which is QUIC.

Q · Mechanism — Why can't HTTP/2 deliver stream 3's complete bytes while stream 1's packet is missing? Because they're not available to it. TCP holds bytes after a gap in the kernel and gives the application only an in-order prefix. So the HTTP/2 parser never sees stream 3's frames. Its streams exist only above that point. That note owns the walk-through.

Q · Trade-off — Would several HTTP/2 connections fix this? Partly, at a price. Each connection is an independent stall domain, so a loss touches a share. But RFC 9113 §9.1 advises one, and you bring back handshakes, cold windows and competing congestion controllers. For a browser, moving to HTTP/3 is the cleaner answer, if your cohorts justify it.

Compare

Property HTTP/1.1 × 6 HTTP/2 × 1 HTTP/3 × 1 When you'd care
Stalled by one loss 1 connection all streams 1 stream lossy paths
Wait between requests yes none none long RTT
Recovery state 6 sets 1 set 1 set, per stream order fairness

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Connections per origin 1 SHOULD NOT open more spec: RFC 9113 §9.1
Losses, 300 packets at 1% 3 expected per page derived
Linux RTO floor 200 ms initial value is 1 s default (as of Nov 2026): Linux, see 022
/b on a shared connection 304 ms vs 1 ms alone relay stand-in, not real loss measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "HTTP/2 fixed head-of-line blocking"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the release notes say so, and it's true at HTTP.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the blocking moved down a layer, and multiplexing widened its scope. Under loss a single connection stalls everything.
    ↳ Think instead: name the layer: HTTP's is gone; TCP's isn't.
  • "So HTTP/2 is worse than HTTP/1.1 on bad networks"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the blast radius is larger, so the conclusion looks automatic.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the outcome depends on RTT, stream count and loss pattern, and HTTP/2 still removes every wait between requests.
    ↳ Think instead: no universal crossover exists; measure your own cohorts.
  • Not the same: a stall vs a bandwidth limit
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both show up as a slow download.
    ↳ Difference: a stall delivers nothing for one RTT or more, and then releases a burst. A window limit paces smoothly.
    ↳ Think instead: look at gaps between chunks, not the average rate.
  • Don't move to HTTP/3 on a hop you haven't measured.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the named fix for this exact flaw.
    ↳ What goes wrong: inside a data centre, loss is rare, so you pay CPU and tooling costs for nothing.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler check: chart p99 against retransmits first, and fix buffering first.
  • Shelf life: permanent over TCP. How often it hurts you changes with your traffic mix.

Connections

Path:HPACK, priorities, pushHTTP/2's remaining flawQUIC
  • Builds on TCP head-of-line blocking: the owner of the mechanism.
  • Contrasts with QUIC: the transport that knows about streams.
  • Composes with head-of-line blocking in four places: this is one of them.
  • Measured by tail latency: why averages hide it.
  • Decided in when each version matters.

notes.title: QUIC — A UDP Transport with TLS 1.3 Inside and Per-Stream Recovery
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9000: QUIC · 📜 RFC 9001: Using TLS to Secure QUIC · 📜 RFC 9002: Loss Detection and Congestion Control · Langley et al., SIGCOMM 2017: The QUIC Transport Protocol · nginx: HTTP/3 module

TL;DR

QUIC rebuilds reliability, ordering and congestion control in a userspace library over UDP, with TLS 1.3 inside the handshake. The transport sees streams, so a lost packet stalls only the stream it carried. You save one setup round trip and the shared stall, and you pay CPU, a blinded capture, and a TCP fallback you must keep.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:Initial with ClientHelloserver Initial + Handshake1 RTTclient Finished + request1 RTTSTREAM frames per streamone packet lostonly that stream waitsdata resent under a new packet number

Recall

Prompt Answer
Round trips to the first response byte: new, then 0-RTT? 2 new; 1 with 0-RTT. TLS over TCP takes 3.
Why UDP? Middleboxes pass it, and the transport can ship in userspace.
What does a retransmission reuse? Nothing of the packet: new packet number, new frames, same stream offset.
What ordering does QUIC promise? Within a stream only; none across streams.
What may a server send before validating an address? At most three times the bytes received.
Draw by hand: handshake, then one lost packet Two flights, then stream 4 delivered, stream 8 waits, resend under a new number.

The idea

A chat app runs a hundred streams over one HTTP/2 connection. A phone loses one packet, and every stream freezes behind it because TCP can only see one byte stream. Fixing that inside TCP means changing kernels and middleboxes worldwide.

So QUIC moves the stream into the transport. The stream ID sits in a STREAM frame the transport itself reads, so a loss touches only that stream. Since a new transport was needed anyway, the TLS handshake moves in as well, and setup drops a trip.

Why UDP? Not for speed. Langley et al. report a firewall classifier breaking on one changed flag bit, which is the ossification QUIC's encryption exists to stop. UDP is the part of the internet that still lets a new transport through.

The trade: per-stream recovery and one fewer round trip, paid in CPU per byte, encrypted headers your tools can't read, and UDP that some networks block.

How it works

A new connection, then one loss. Transport parameters ride inside the TLS messages, so crypto and transport finish together.

The transport never stops delivering 4 and 12, because the gap belongs to 8 alone. The packet is laid out so that only a little stays visible:

 1-RTT packet, short header
 +-+-+-+---+-+---+
 |0|1|S|R R|K|P P|   header form, fixed bit, spin, reserved, key phase, PN length
 +-+-+-+---+-+---+
 | Destination Connection ID (0..160 bits) |  identity, not the 4-tuple
 +-----------------------------------------+
 | Packet Number (8..32 bits)              |  never reused in a number space
 +-----------------------------------------+
 | Packet Payload: frames, e.g. STREAM     |  stream ID and offset, encrypted
 +-----------------------------------------+

RFC 9000 §17.3.1; RFC 9001 §5.4 masks the packet number and the low five bits of the first byte.

Rule What actually happens
Handshake RFC 9000 §7 carries TLS in CRYPTO frames. TLS older than 1.3 must not be offered. There's no unencrypted QUIC, though Initial keys derive from the connection ID, so Initial isn't confidential.
Packet numbers Monotonic per number space and never reused. Lost data goes in new frames in a new packet, so an ACK names one transmission unambiguously.
0-RTT Early data has no replay protection between connections. The TLS 1.3 handshake owns the rules; keep it to safe, idempotent requests.
Where the round trips go Setup is one, so the request's own trip makes 2. The handshake table owns the comparison, and the budget the arithmetic.
Who in the middle acts on this Middleboxes see UDP and a connection ID. A balancer routes by ID (migration); a firewall may drop UDP 443, so clients fall back to TCP.

Evolution

Lineage:2017 Google reports 7% of internet traffic on its QUIC2021 RFC 9000, 9001, 90022022 HTTP/3 (RFC 9114)2023 QUIC v2 (RFC 9369)2026 multipath in the RFC Editor queue
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Nov 2026): widely deployed at edges, while tooling, kernel offloads and balancer support still move. nginx still labels its module experimental.
  • Changed in RFC 9000 (May 2021): the IETF design replaced Google's wire format, so older "QUIC" material may describe an incompatible protocol.
  • What's next: multipath and QUIC-LB are drafts. What won't change: per-stream order, and that some networks block UDP.

On the wire

No QUIC server is installed here, and curl 8.7.1 has no HTTP/3. Go 1.27.3's standard crypto/tls does run the QUIC TLS handshake, in memory. Captured on 1 Nov 2026 with a local self-signed certificate; there's no UDP, so these are CRYPTO bytes, not packets:

flight 1 client -> server  Initial: 1470                  # ① ClientHello
  server got peer transport params "client-tp"            # inside ClientHello
flight 2 server -> client  Initial: 1178, Handshake: 540  # ②
  client got peer transport params "server-tp"
  client can now WRITE at Application                     # keys after one round trip
  client handshake done
flight 3 client -> server  Handshake: 36                  # ③ Finished, joined by the request
negotiated: h3 304                                        # TLS 0x0304 = 1.3

Two flights yield keys, which is the one setup trip. The request leaves with flight 3, so the response arrives one round trip later.

Break it: does an ACK tell you the RTT? Here the original is delayed, the sender resends needlessly at 100 ms, and an ACK arrives at 160 ms:

send_orig, send_retx, ack_at = 0, 100, 160            # the original did arrive
tcp = (ack_at - send_orig, ack_at - send_retx)        # same seq number: which send?
pkts = {7: send_orig, 8: send_retx}                   # QUIC: the resend is a new number
acked = 7                                             # the ACK names packet 7
print("TCP candidates:", tcp, "QUIC sample:", ack_at - pkts[acked])
# look for: two possible RTT samples on TCP, one on QUIC
# naive belief predicts: every ACK gives one clean RTT sample

Run on Python 3.15.0: TCP candidates: (160, 60) QUIC sample: 160. This is arithmetic, not a capture. TCP needs timestamps or Karn's rule to avoid the bad sample; QUIC's numbering removes the ambiguity.

Measure it

  • See it: curl --http3-only -w '%{http_version}' on a curl built with HTTP/3 (illustrative here) prints 3; qlog shows packet numbers and loss, since captures can't without keys.
  • In production: per region and ASN, share of requests on h3; per connection, handshake failures and fallback; per protocol, edge CPU per gigabit and UDP receive-buffer drops.
  • Bounded by: UDP blocked or QUIC misbehaving → a TCP path offered at all times, a short Alt-Svc ma for rollback, and 0-RTT limited to safe requests.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: QUIC is a transport in userspace over UDP, with TLS 1.3 built in. Because the transport carries streams, one lost packet stalls one stream, not the connection. Setup takes one round trip, so the first response byte arrives after two, against three for TLS over TCP. UDP was chosen for deployability, not speed, and QUIC costs more CPU than TCP, so I'd measure before committing.

Q · Mechanism — What's the difference between a packet number and a stream offset? A packet number identifies one transmission and only ever rises. A stream offset says where bytes belong in a stream. TCP's sequence number does both jobs, which is why a retransmission is ambiguous. QUIC separates them: lost data is resent under a new packet number at its old offset, so loss detection gets clean RTT samples, and a stream reassembles by offset regardless of arrival order.

Q · Trade-off — 0-RTT saves a round trip. When would you refuse it? Whenever a replay would do harm. Early data can be captured and resent, and the server can't prove it's fresh because no round trip has happened. A cacheable GET tolerates that. A POST that moves money doesn't, and neither does anything that consumes a token. So accept it per request at the edge, not per connection, and reject or delay the rest until the handshake completes. Mobile saves most, since it reconnects often.

Q · Failure — You enable HTTP/3 and edge CPU rises with no change in request rate. What's happening? Clients moved to a path with more per-byte work, so a capacity model keyed to requests stops predicting. Google reported about 3.5 times TLS/TCP's CPU on YouTube traffic at first, and about twice on web traffic after optimisation (2017, its own stack). Confirm with CPU per gigabit split by protocol and UDP receive errors. Fix with UDP segmentation offload where supported, larger socket buffers, and a fleet sized for the mix.

Q · Design — Sequence an HTTP/3 rollout for a global consumer product. The binding constraint is a benefit concentrated in lossy, long-RTT cohorts and a cost spread across the fleet. First measure p99 by network type and version. Then enable one edge location with a short Alt-Svc lifetime, route by connection ID, and keep HTTP/2 over TCP to the origin. Watch h3 share first: quiet fallback looks like success. When each version matters owns the decision, deployment and observability the staged rollout.

Compare

Property TLS 1.3 over TCP QUIC When you'd pick it
Setup 2 RTT 1 RTT QUIC when reconnects are frequent
Loss scope connection stream QUIC on lossy paths
Identity 4-tuple connection ID QUIC when clients roam
Lives in kernel + library library QUIC to ship changes fast
Capture headers readable needs keys or qlog TCP when debugging tools matter
Reachability near universal UDP may be blocked TCP as the permanent fallback

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Setup, new 1 RTT 2 to first response byte spec: RFC 9000 §7; derived
Minimum datagram path 1,200 bytes client pads Initial to this spec: RFC 9000 §14
Unvalidated send limit 3× bytes received anti-amplification spec: RFC 9000 §8.1
Connection ID, v1 0–20 bytes server chooses what it receives spec: RFC 9000 §17.2
0-RTT ticket age ≤ 7 days TLS limit spec: RFC 9001 §4.6
Server CPU vs TLS/TCP ≈ 3.5×, then ≈ 2× Google's stack, 2017; don't apply to yours measured: Langley et al. §6.7
Clients unable to use QUIC 4.4% Nov 2016, Google video playbacks measured: Langley et al. §7.2

Pitfalls

  • "QUIC is faster because UDP is lighter"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: UDP has the reputation for speed, and QUIC runs on it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: QUIC rebuilds reliability, ordering and congestion control, and costs more CPU per byte than TCP. The gains are one setup trip and a smaller stall.
    ↳ Think instead: UDP is a route through the middle, not an optimisation.
  • "QUIC removes head-of-line blocking"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the headline claim in every comparison.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: order still holds inside a stream, so a loss stalls that stream. RFC 9000 only drops order across streams. One big download gets nothing.
    ↳ Think instead: the blast radius moved from the connection to the stream.
  • "0-RTT means zero round trips to a response"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the name reads like a latency figure.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it names setup. The request can leave in the first flight, and the response still needs one RTT, so 1 RTT to first byte, and only on resumption.
    ↳ Think instead: count to the first response byte: 3, 2, 1.
  • Not the same: Google QUIC vs IETF QUIC
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: same name, same origin, and older articles rarely say which.
    ↳ Difference: Google's deployed protocol came first, and the 2017 numbers describe it. RFC 9000 is a redesigned, incompatible protocol using TLS 1.3.
    ↳ Think instead: date any measurement, and ask which QUIC it describes.
  • Don't run QUIC where TCP would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the newest transport, and uniform stacks look tidy.
    ↳ What goes wrong: on a clean, low-delay hop such as a backbone, there's little to gain. Google reports little gain and sometimes a loss on low-loss, low-delay networks, while you pay CPU and lose tooling.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: HTTP/2 over TCP inside your network, QUIC at the edge.
  • Shelf life: the RFC 9000 rules are durable. CPU ratios, UDP blocking and product support age fast, so quote them with a date or not at all.

Connections

Path:HTTP/2's remaining flawQUICconnection migrationHTTP/3
  • Builds on when UDP is right: UDP as a substrate.
  • Owned elsewhere: head-of-line blocking owns why TCP stalls; the TLS 1.3 handshake owns 0-RTT replay.
  • Bounded by ALPN and Alt-Svc: the TCP fallback and rollback lever.
  • Contrasts with the TCP handshake: setup per layer against setup in one.
  • Used by HTTP/3 and WebTransport: streams they no longer build themselves.
  • Decided in when each version matters: which hop earns it.

notes.title: Connection Migration in QUIC
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9000 §9: Connection Migration · 📜 RFC 9000 §5.1: Connection ID · AWS: QUIC listeners for Network Load Balancers · IETF: QUIC-LB draft

TL;DR

TCP names a connection by its 4-tuple, so a new address ends it. QUIC names it by a connection ID, so a client can change network and keep its streams, its keys and its data in flight. The price falls on the middle: a balancer must route by connection ID, and a 4-tuple hash sends a migrated client to the wrong server.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:Wi-Fi dropsclient sends from cellularnew connection ID, same connectionserver sends PATH_CHALLENGEclient answerspath validatedcongestion state resetstreams continue

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which side can migrate? Only the client. A server can offer a preferred address at the handshake.
Why validate the new path? So nobody can aim server traffic at a victim's address.
Why a fresh connection ID on the new path? So an observer can't link the two paths.

The idea

You walk out of the office in the middle of a voice call. Your phone leaves Wi-Fi for cellular. The source address changes, so every TCP connection ends, and the app has to reconnect: handshake, TLS, cold window, and an in-flight request whose fate is unknown.

QUIC keeps nothing in the 4-tuple. Packets carry a connection ID, so the server recognises the connection from a new address and carries on. NAT rebinding, which happens without the client knowing, gets the same treatment.

The benefit depends on the middle. If a balancer hashes the 4-tuple, the next packet lands on another server, which has no keys. Migration works only if the path to the server can follow the ID.

The trade: survival across networks, paid in balancer support and in path validation before full-speed sending.

How it works

The client moves first, and the server validates before trusting the new path.

Rule What actually happens
Connection IDs Each end issues spares with NEW_CONNECTION_ID. An ID must not be reused across local addresses (§9.5), which stops linking.
Validation §8.2 needs a PATH_CHALLENGE and matching PATH_RESPONSE; until then sends stay under the three-times limit of §8.1.
Congestion state §9.4 resets the controller and RTT estimate on a new path; a port-only change may keep them.
Where the round trips go About 1 RTT for validation, against 2 RTT plus a cold window for new TCP and TLS 1.3.
Who in the middle acts on this A balancer must route by connection ID. A server can refuse with disable_active_migration (§5.2.3).

Evolution

Lineage:2021 RFC 9000 §92025 AWS NLB QUIC passthrough2026 QUIC-LB draft-22, multipath in the RFC Editor queue
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Nov 2026): the spec is settled, while balancers are catching up. NLB's QUIC listeners route by an 8-byte Server ID. CloudFront's HTTP/3 documentation says it supports migration.
  • Changed in Nov 2025: AWS NLB added QUIC passthrough with stickiness by connection ID. QUIC-LB, the shared routing standard, is still an active draft with no RFC.
  • What won't change: something has to map an opaque ID to a server, and the server chose the ID.

On the wire

No QUIC server is installed here, so this is the identity logic alone: a stdlib UDP receiver on 127.0.0.1 keeps two tables, by 4-tuple and by a connection ID in the payload. The client changes source port halfway. Captured on 1 Nov 2026 with Python 3.15.0, as a model, not as QUIC:

port 52630  packet 1   4-tuple count 1   connection ID count 1
port 52630  packet 2   4-tuple count 2   connection ID count 2
port 53033  packet 3   4-tuple count 1   connection ID count 3
port 53033  packet 4   4-tuple count 2   connection ID count 4

The 4-tuple view sees a new connection at packet 3. The ID view sees the same one. On the 4-tuple view, connection state has gone, which is what TCP and a hashing balancer both do.

Measure it

  • See it: a qlog on the client marks path changes, with PATH_CHALLENGE and PATH_RESPONSE; a capture can't, since those frames are encrypted.
  • In production: per client platform, migrations attempted against completed; connection resets for unknown connection ID at servers; requests that fail across a network change.
  • Bounded by: a balancer that loses the connection → route by ID, or a server-issued ID scheme, and accept reconnect as the fallback, since Stateless Reset (§10.3) ends the connection cleanly.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: TCP identifies a connection by its 4-tuple, so a network change kills it. QUIC identifies it by a connection ID, so a client can change address and keep streams and keys. The server validates the new path first, to prevent traffic being aimed at a victim. A balancer has to route by that ID, or the packets reach a server that has no state.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a client switch connection IDs when it moves? Privacy. If the ID stayed, anyone watching both networks could link the two paths to one user. So peers issue spare IDs ahead of time with NEW_CONNECTION_ID, and §9.5 forbids using one from more than one local address. That creates the balancer problem: the new ID must still route to the same server, so the server encodes routing information in IDs it issues.

Q · Trade-off — Does migration make a voice call seamless? It saves the connection, not the moment. The client still needs to notice the old path failed, and the new path starts with a reset congestion controller and an RTT unknown. Expect a stall, shorter than a full reconnect. Application state survives, which is the real gain: no replayed requests and no new handshake. Measure gaps across real handovers.

Compare

Property TCP QUIC, with ID routing QUIC, 4-tuple hash When you'd care
Address change connection dies connection continues wrong server, reset mobile clients
NAT rebinding connection dies continues wrong server long idle flows
Cost after moving 2 RTT + cold window validation, reset window new connection handovers

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Connection ID length 0–20 bytes QUIC v1 spec: RFC 9000 §17.2
Sends before validation 3× received anti-amplification spec: RFC 9000 §8.1
NLB Server ID 8 bytes QUIC listeners default (as of Nov 2026): AWS NLB
Identity tables at new port 1 vs 3 4-tuple vs ID measured: Python 3.15.0, 1 Nov 2026, model

Pitfalls

  • "Migration gives you zero downtime on a network change"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the connection does survive, so it sounds seamless.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: path validation and a reset congestion controller still take time, and the client must first notice the old path failed.
    ↳ Think instead: no reconnect, but a short stall.
  • "Either end can migrate"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: QUIC seems symmetric.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: RFC 9000 §9 allows only clients to migrate. A server can offer a preferred address at the handshake (§9.6), and that's all.
    ↳ Think instead: clients move; servers suggest.
  • Not the same: migration vs multipath
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both involve two networks.
    ↳ Difference: migration uses one path at a time. Multipath uses several at once, and in Nov 2026 it's approved but has no RFC number.
    ↳ Think instead: replace vs combine.
  • Don't count on migration behind a 4-tuple balancer.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: HTTP/3 works in testing, and QUIC "supports migration".
    ↳ What goes wrong: a client on a static test network never moves, so you only find out in production.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler honest position: set disable_active_migration until ID routing is in place.
  • Shelf life: RFC 9000's rules are stable. Balancer support and QUIC-LB's status change fast, so re-check before relying on them.

Connections

Path:QUICconnection migrationHTTP/3
  • Builds on QUIC: packets carry an ID, not a 4-tuple identity.
  • Contrasts with sockets and ports: the 4-tuple identity it leaves.
  • Used by when each version matters: mobile apps' strongest argument.
  • Composes with L4 vs L7 balancing: it needs ID routing.

notes.title: HTTP/3 — HTTP Semantics over QUIC
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9114: HTTP/3 · 📜 RFC 9204: QPACK · 📜 RFC 7838: HTTP Alternative Services · nginx: HTTP/3 module

TL;DR

HTTP/3 is HTTP's same meaning on QUIC. Because QUIC already provides streams and flow control, HTTP/3 deletes those parts of HTTP/2 and keeps only what's left: headers and data. The new work is QPACK, a header table that doesn't force the in-order delivery QUIC just removed.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
