Flow:client learns h3QUIC connectscontrol stream + QPACK streams openrequest on a bidirectional streamHEADERS + DATAstream ends

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which HTTP/2 frames are gone? PRIORITY, RST_STREAM, WINDOW_UPDATE, PING, CONTINUATION: QUIC does those jobs.
How does a client first discover HTTP/3? Alt-Svc, or an HTTPS DNS record.
Why isn't HPACK reused? It assumes in-order delivery, which QUIC streams don't give across streams.

The idea

HTTP/2 built streams on TCP, so it needed its own stream IDs, flow control, cancellation and pings. Once QUIC provides those in the transport, keeping them above it would duplicate everything. So HTTP/3 becomes a thin mapping: each request takes a QUIC stream, and only HEADERS and DATA frames remain on it.

One thing couldn't transfer. HPACK's table works because headers arrive in order. On HTTP/3, a request that adds a table entry can arrive after one that references it, and a shared in-order path would rebuild the blocking QUIC removed. QPACK sends table updates on their own streams, and lets a request say which table state it needs.

A client also can't assume a server speaks HTTP/3. TCP gets a port and ALPN. HTTP/3 needs a way to learn that UDP is worth trying, and a discovery step.

The trade: a thinner HTTP layer on a heavier transport, and a choice between compression and blocking on every encoder.

How it works

One connection holds request streams and a few unidirectional helpers.

Rule What actually happens
Mapping RFC 9114 §4.1: one request-response per client-initiated bidirectional stream. Its end marks the message's end.
QPACK RFC 9204: 99 static entries. BLOCKED_STREAMS defaults to 0, so by default an encoder may not send references a decoder lacks.
Push Defined in §4.6, but a client must first send MAX_PUSH_ID, so it's opt-in; see push's history.
Where the round trips go One setup on a new connection, then one per request; the first visit may start on TCP until the client learns h3.
Who in the middle acts on this UDP 443 must pass, and failing that §3.1 tells clients to try TCP. A balancer routes by connection ID.

Evolution

Lineage:2021 QUIC (RFC 9000)2022 HTTP/3 and QPACK (RFC 9114, 9204)2023 HTTPS records (RFC 9460)2025 AWS NLB passes QUIC
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Nov 2026): normal at large edges. nginx still calls ngx_http_v3_module experimental, and AWS ALB's listener documentation doesn't mention HTTP/3.
  • Changed in RFC 9114 (Jun 2022): frame type numbers follow HTTP/2 where possible, and HTTP/2's removed types are reserved (§7.2.8) so they can't be sent by mistake.
  • What's next: wider edge support, and tooling; curl's --http3 falls back to older versions, while --http3-only doesn't. What won't change: a TCP path stays necessary.

On the wire

Illustrative, with no timings: the shape RFC 9114 defines on a request stream.

QUIC STREAM id=0  (client bidi)  HEADERS  :method GET, :path /
QUIC STREAM id=0  (server)       HEADERS  :status 200
QUIC STREAM id=0  (server)       DATA     body
QUIC STREAM id=0  FIN                     ← the stream's end marks the message's end
QUIC STREAM id=2  (client uni)   control: SETTINGS
QUIC STREAM id=6  (client uni)   QPACK encoder
QUIC STREAM id=10 (client uni)   QPACK decoder

There's no stream field inside an HTTP/3 frame, because the QUIC stream is the identity. The QUIC note shows the handshake that was captured.

Measure it

  • See it: curl --http3-only -sI -w '%{http_version}\n' https://example.com on a build with HTTP/3 (illustrative here); devtools' Protocol column shows h3.
  • In production: per region and ASN, share of h3 requests; per listener, QPACK blocked streams and fallback rate.
  • Bounded by: UDP blocked → a TCP listener at all times, and a short ma on Alt-Svc so a bad rollout clears itself.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: HTTP/3 keeps HTTP's semantics, and moves them onto QUIC. QUIC owns streams, flow control and cancellation, so HTTP/3 keeps only HEADERS and DATA, one request per QUIC stream. HPACK needed in-order delivery, so QPACK replaces it, with separate streams for table updates. Discovery needs Alt-Svc or an HTTPS record, and TCP stays as fallback.

Q · Mechanism — Why couldn't HPACK be reused? HPACK encodes table changes inside header blocks and assumes they're decoded in the order sent. That was safe on TCP. On QUIC, streams arrive independently, so one block can reference an entry another hasn't delivered yet. Forcing order would rebuild the shared stall. QPACK puts updates on dedicated streams, and each block states the insert count it needs.

Q · Trade-off — What does BLOCKED_STREAMS trade? Compression against blocking. Allowing blocked streams lets an encoder reference fresh entries, so headers shrink, but a stream can wait for a table update. At the default of 0, an encoder uses only acknowledged entries, so there's no blocking, and less compression early on. Small default, safe behaviour: raise it only if you've measured header bytes as a real cost.

Compare

Concern HTTP/2 HTTP/3 When you'd care
Streams HTTP layer QUIC stall scope
Flow control WINDOW_UPDATE QUIC frames proxy tuning
Cancel RST_STREAM QUIC RESET_STREAM deadlines
Headers HPACK QPACK header-heavy APIs
Discovery ALPN on TCP Alt-Svc, HTTPS record first visit

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
QPACK static entries 99 against 61 in HPACK spec: RFC 9204
BLOCKED_STREAMS 0 by default no blocking unless raised spec: RFC 9204
QPACK stream types 0x02, 0x03 encoder, decoder spec: RFC 9204
ALPN token h3 QUIC v1 spec: RFC 9114 §3.1
nginx stream limit 128 http3_max_concurrent_streams default (as of Nov 2026): nginx
Alt-Svc default lifetime 24 hours ma spec: RFC 7838

Pitfalls

  • "HTTP/3 is a new HTTP"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the major number changed again.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: methods, status codes and caching are RFC 9110, as before. The change is mapping and transport.
    ↳ Think instead: same meaning on a different transport.
  • "The first visit always uses TCP"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: with Alt-Svc alone, it does: the header comes over TCP.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: an HTTPS DNS record (RFC 9460) can advertise h3 before any connection, so the first one can be QUIC.
    ↳ Think instead: discovery has two routes; count both.
  • Not the same: HPACK vs QPACK
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: same idea, similar names, one letter apart.
    ↳ Difference: HPACK updates tables inline and relies on order. QPACK separates updates, and each block states what it needs.
    ↳ Think instead: QPACK is HPACK with the ordering dependency removed.
  • Don't turn on HTTP/3 without a TCP listener beside it.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: HTTP/3-only looks clean, and it works from your laptop.
    ↳ What goes wrong: clients on UDP-blocking networks can't reach you. RFC 9114 §3.1 expects a TCP attempt on failure, and there'd be none to try.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler rule: keep HTTP/2 on the same name, always.
  • Shelf life: the RFC mapping is stable. Product support moves, so check the chapter map's Landscape.

Connections

Path:connection migrationHTTP/3when each version matters
  • Builds on QUIC: streams, flow control, cancellation.
  • Evolved from HPACK: QPACK removes the ordering dependency.
  • Contrasts with HTTP/2 framing: the frames that were left behind.
  • Discovered by ALPN and Alt-Svc: how a client learns to try.
  • Composes with WebTransport: streams exposed to applications.

notes.title: When Each HTTP Version Actually Matters
notes.html:
References

Langley et al., SIGCOMM 2017: The QUIC Transport Protocol · Cloudflare, Apr 2020: Comparing HTTP/3 vs HTTP/2 · 📜 RFC 9113: HTTP/2 · 📜 RFC 9114: HTTP/3 · HPBN: HTTP/2

TL;DR

Each version removes one bottleneck, so the right question is which bottleneck this hop has. HTTP/2 deletes the wait between requests; HTTP/3 deletes the shared stall under loss and one setup trip. Version is a property of a hop, not of a company, and a hop without that bottleneck gets only the cost.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:pick the hopconcurrent requests?HTTP/1.1measured loss-driven tail?HTTP/2UDP, ID routing, CPU?HTTP/3 with HTTP/2 fallback

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does HTTP/2's gain scale with? requests × RTT, the rounds it deletes.
What does HTTP/3's gain scale with? Loss × streams on the connection, plus one setup RTT.
Where's a gain near zero? One request at a time, or a clean, short hop.
Which percentile shows HTTP/3's win? The tail of a cohort, not the mean.
Is there a universal loss rate where HTTP/3 wins? No. Measure your own cohorts.
Draw by hand: the per-hop decision tree Concurrency? then loss-driven tail? then UDP reachable? Default HTTP/1.1, then HTTP/2.

The idea

Five decisions, each as checks, answer and defence. Inputs are illustrative; the arithmetic is not.

  • A web app, 94 requests per page, 210 ms from its origin, three shard hostnames. Check concurrency, RTT, sharding → HTTP/2, an edge nearby, sharding removed. Defence: 210 ms × ceil(94 ÷ 6) is about 3.4 s of round trips, and HTTP/2 deletes that term.
  • "Move the internal gRPC mesh to HTTP/3?" Check pod-to-pod loss, tail against median, sidecar CPU → no, stay on HTTP/2. Defence: no loss means nothing to recover, and CPU cost is real.
  • A token stream stutters for some users, dashboard green. Check proxy_buffering, then segment by network type, then retransmits → fix the proxy first; HTTP/3 only if it's transport. Defence: one is a config line, the other a platform project (buffering proxies).
  • A webhook sender to thousands of customer endpoints. Check per-endpoint concurrency, who owns the receiver, debugging needs → HTTP/1.1 with a pool. Defence: no concurrency to multiplex, and curl -v reproduces a customer's failure.
  • Marketing wants HTTP/3 in two weeks. Check per-cohort measurement, balancer routing, UDP 443 → sequence it: measure, route, one location. Defence: without measurement you can't tell whether it helped.

The trade: each upgrade buys one specific win and pays with moving parts, so an upgrade on the wrong hop is pure cost.

How it works

The binding question is whether the hop has concurrency at all, and HTTP/1.1 is the default every other leaf has to earn its way past.

  • HTTP/1.1: changes when callers issue concurrent requests to one origin; then rounds appear.
  • HTTP/2: changes when a cohort's tail tracks retransmits, and the middle can pass UDP.
  • HTTP/3: changes when fallback share stays high; then you're paying for nothing.
Workload Pick Why Expected gain
Web page, 100+ assets, long RTT HTTP/2, then HTTP/3 deletes RTT × ceil(n ÷ 6) large
Same page, all users on a LAN HTTP/2, don't expect much the term is already tiny small
Mobile app, frequent reconnects HTTP/3 one less trip per connect, stalls per stream, migration largest in the tail
One large file any one stream has nothing to multiplex near zero
LLM tokens to consumers HTTP/3 at the edge sparse writes land on slower recovery paths tail, once proxies are clean
gRPC in one region HTTP/2 (required) fewer connections; loss negligible operational
gRPC across regions, VPN HTTP/2, watch p99 unrelated calls share stalls mixed: measure
Service to service, no concurrency HTTP/1.1 simple, readable near zero
Edge to origin, backbone HTTP/2 over TCP no last-mile loss, cheaper CPU near zero for HTTP/3
Webhook, cron, CLI HTTP/1.1 no concurrency; you may not own the receiver near zero

Two expressions generate every row. Keep them, and the table rebuilds itself:

gain 1.1 → 2 ≈ RTT · ceil(n ÷ 6)                ← 120 at 200 ms = 4 s; 8 at 20 ms = 40 ms
gain 2 → 3   ≈ 1 RTT per new connection + shared stalls avoided
stalls       ≈ packets · loss, each one stalling all streams on TCP   ← 300 · 1% = 3

The first is owned by HTTP/1.1's limits and the second by HTTP/2's flaw.

Evolution

Lineage:1997 HTTP/1.12015 HTTP/2 (RFC 7540)2021 QUIC (RFC 9000)2022 RFC 9110–91142025 AWS NLB passes QUIC
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Nov 2026): HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 are settled, while HTTP/3's support in balancers and tools still moves (Landscape).
  • Changed in RFC 9113 and 9114 (Jun 2022): priorities moved to RFC 9218, and all three versions now share RFC 9110, so changing version per hop can't change meaning.
  • What's next: more client traffic on HTTP/3, and balancers routing by connection ID. What won't change: a version only removes a bottleneck you have.

On the wire

Captured on 1 Nov 2026: curl 8.7.1 on 127.0.0.1 over TLS 1.3, against a stdlib HTTP/1.1 server and a small stdlib HTTP/2 server (Python 3.15.0). Each response sleeps 20 ms to stand in for a round trip. Medians of 5 runs:

                       HTTP/1.1, 6 conns    HTTP/2, 1 conn
120 small responses         504 ms              45 ms
1 small response             36 ms              34 ms
1 download, 8 MiB            42 ms              60 ms

The first row is the term in the formula: 20 ms × 20 rounds = 400 ms, plus setup and Python. The last row is one stream on loopback, where the HTTP/2 figure reflects my Python frame loop, not the protocol: read it as "no gain".

Break it: does a newer version always win? Run the same pair with n as the variable:

python3 t.py     # runs each of these 5 times, then prints the median
curl -sk --http1.1 -Z --parallel-max 6 'https://127.0.0.1:8460/d[1-120]' -o /dev/null
curl -sk --http2 -Z --parallel-max 120 'https://127.0.0.1:8461/d[1-120]' -o /dev/null
curl -sk --http1.1 https://127.0.0.1:8460/d1 -o /dev/null          # n = 1
curl -sk --http2   https://127.0.0.1:8461/d1 -o /dev/null
# look for: a large gap at n = 120, none at n = 1
# naive belief predicts: HTTP/2 wins by the same factor at every n

Run on the servers above: an elevenfold gap at 120, and 36 against 34 ms at 1. Concurrency was the only variable, so the win is the term, not the version.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -w '%{http_version} %{time_starttransfer}' per hop; in devtools the Protocol column, per request, shows http/1.1, h2 or h3.
  • In production: per cohort, p99 and p50 by network type and negotiated version; per region and ASN, h3 share; per backend, request skew; per protocol, CPU per gigabit.
  • Bounded by: a version change that quietly gives nothing or breaks balancing → log version per request, keep the TCP fallback, a maximum connection age, and a pre-agreed result that stops the rollout.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: The versions fix different bottlenecks. HTTP/2 removes the wait between requests, so it wins with many requests on long paths and does little for a single download. HTTP/3 removes the shared stall under loss and one setup trip, so it shows up in a mobile cohort's tail, at higher CPU. I'd pick per hop, starting from what that hop's traffic is short of.

Q · Mechanism — Name a case where HTTP/2 buys nothing, and why. A single large download. HTTP/2's gain is deleting rounds between requests, and one request has no rounds to delete, so the transfer stays bounded by the window and the path, which TCP owns on both versions. Our local run agrees: 36 against 34 ms for one request, 504 against 45 ms for 120. A cron job has the same property, for the same reason.

Q · Trade-off — Argue against enabling HTTP/3. If traffic is mostly fixed-line, there's little tail to improve. Google's 2017 data shows gains shrink as RTT and loss fall: search latency down 13.2% on desktop in India, 1.3% in South Korea, on its own stack. Cloudflare's 2020 test had HTTP/3 ahead on first byte and about even on load. Against that sit CPU, UDP through the middle, and a second path to debug. So: build cohort measurement first, set a trigger, spend on edge placement meanwhile.

Q · Failure — A quarter of clients sit behind UDP-blocking firewalls. What breaks? Nothing, which is the problem. Those clients try QUIC, fail, and use TCP; every request succeeds. What runs out is the return on the fleet you sized for HTTP/3, and the dashboard symptom is an absence: h3 share plateaus low on particular networks. Confirm by charting negotiated version per ASN. Then get UDP 443 opened for those customers, or document that they stay on HTTP/2. Without per-request version logs you never see it.

Q · Design — Give a protocol strategy for browsers, mobile apps and internal services. One answer per hop. Browser and app to edge: HTTP/3 offered, HTTP/2 fallback, because the last mile has the loss. Edge to origin: HTTP/2 over TCP, since a backbone doesn't need per-stream recovery. Service to service: HTTP/2 where concurrency or gRPC needs it, otherwise HTTP/1.1. Webhooks: HTTP/1.1. Terminate multiplexed hops at L7, and recycle connections. Watch request skew first. Service communication patterns covers the call shape.

Compare

Version Removes Costs Who in the middle must change When you'd pick it
HTTP/1.1 nothing, the baseline a wait per request nothing low concurrency, readable wire
HTTP/2 rounds between requests one failure domain L7 balancing, connection age concurrency over TCP
HTTP/3 shared stall, one setup RTT CPU, tooling, two paths UDP 443, ID routing measured lossy cohorts

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
120 responses, 20 ms each 504 ms vs 45 ms HTTP/1.1 six connections vs HTTP/2 measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026
1 response, same delay 36 ms vs 34 ms nothing to multiplex measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026
120 assets at 200 ms 4,000 ms of rounds RTT × ceil(n ÷ 6) derived
Search latency gain, desktop 13.2% India, 3.4% USA, 1.3% South Korea Google's QUIC, 2017 measured: Langley et al. Table 3
First byte, Cloudflare test 176 ms vs 201 ms HTTP/3 vs HTTP/2, 2020, different congestion control measured: Cloudflare, Apr 2020

Pitfalls

  • "Above 2% loss, HTTP/3 beats HTTP/2"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a single threshold makes a tidy rule, and older notes attributed it to Cloudflare.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: Cloudflare's Apr 2020 post states no such figure, and we found no primary source. The result depends on RTT, stream count and congestion control.
    ↳ Think instead: no universal crossover exists; measure your cohorts, by network type and version.
  • "Newer versions are faster, so upgrade everywhere"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: version numbers suggest strict improvement, and vendors quote percentages.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: each version removes one bottleneck. On a hop without it, you get no gain and keep the cost, as with HTTP/3 on a backbone.
    ↳ Think instead: pick per hop, from that hop's traffic and loss.
  • "We tried HTTP/2 and saw nothing, so it's overhyped"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a real test produced a flat graph.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the gain is requests × RTT. A LAN test, a low-concurrency workload or leftover sharding each hides it.
    ↳ Think instead: test on a long path with real concurrency, one connection per origin.
  • Not the same: HTTP/2's win vs HTTP/3's win
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are sold as "faster" in one chart.
    ↳ Difference: HTTP/2's applies to every page with concurrency, so medians move. HTTP/3's applies on loss or a new connection, so a cohort's tail moves.
    ↳ Think instead: judge each with its own metric, never an aggregate mean.
  • Don't start with a protocol change when placement would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a protocol feels like the engineering answer, and a flag is quick.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a fixed RTT multiplies everything, so a version change can leave a far user slow.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler lever first: terminate at an edge, which shrinks every term.
  • Don't roll out without per-request version logs.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: negotiation is automatic, and traffic keeps flowing.
    ↳ What goes wrong: silent fallback and pinned connections both pass every health check.
    ↳ Do instead: log negotiated version per request, then segment latency by it.
  • Shelf life: the two expressions are durable. Measurements, CPU ratios and blocking rates age, so re-measure them.

Connections

Path:HTTP/3when each version mattersgRPC on HTTP/2
  • Builds on HTTP/1.1's limits and HTTP/2's flaw: the two expressions.
  • Owned elsewhere: head-of-line blocking owns the stall; the handshake owns setup round trips.
  • Bounded by gRPC and HTTP/2 balancing: a multiplexed hop needs it.
  • Composes with CDN and edge: placement compounds with any version.
  • Contrasts with the API choice framework: the same reasoning one layer up.
  • Measured by tail latency: the segmentation discipline.

notes.title: gRPC's Dependence on HTTP/2 — and the Load-Balancing Problem
notes.html:
References

gRPC over HTTP/2 · 📜 RFC 9113 §8.1: HTTP Message Framing · gRPC: Load balancing · gRPC-Web

TL;DR

gRPC maps one call to one HTTP/2 stream, and it reports the outcome in trailers, which arrive after the body. That's why it can't fall back to HTTP/1.1 and why browsers can't speak it directly. Calls share one long-lived connection, so anything balancing by connection will pin them to one backend.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:POST /Service/MethodHEADERS with application/grpcDATA, 5-byte prefix + messageresponse HEADERSDATAtrailing HEADERS with grpc-statusEND_STREAM

Recall

Prompt Answer
Where does a gRPC status live? In trailers, always, not in the HTTP status.
What's the 5-byte prefix? 1 byte compressed flag, 4 bytes message length.
What does a cancelled call send? RST_STREAM, ending one stream only.

The idea

A streaming call doesn't know its outcome when it starts. The server sends messages for minutes, then fails on the last one. A status in the first line can't express that, so gRPC puts the real status at the end, in trailers, which HTTP/2 carries as a final HEADERS frame.

That's the dependence. HTTP/2 gives gRPC several streams at once, cheap cancel, flow control, and trailers that work by default. HTTP/1.1 defines trailers but needs chunked bodies, and it can't interleave calls. Browsers expose no raw trailers to JavaScript, hence gRPC-Web.

The load-balancing problem comes with it. One connection carries thousands of calls, so a connection-level balancer makes one decision for all of them. That note owns the fix; gRPC in production owns the operating side.

The trade: long-lived multiplexing and in-band status, in exchange for depending on a stack that reads HTTP/2 end to end.

How it works

A unary call on the wire: the HTTP status says the transport worked, and the trailer says the call did.

Rule What actually happens
Mapping Path is /Service/Method, content type application/grpc, method always POST. A deadline travels as grpc-timeout.
Message prefix Every message has 1 + 4 bytes in front, so messages don't align to DATA frames and streaming works over any frame split.
Trailers-Only A call that fails at once sends one HEADERS frame holding status and END_STREAM.
Where the round trips go Connection setup happens once. A call then costs 1 RTT, and streams need no further trips.
Who in the middle acts on this An L7 proxy parses HTTP/2 and places each call. An L4 balancer places the connection, so see balancing.

Evolution

Lineage:2015 HTTP/2 (RFC 7540)2017 gRPC's load-balancing guidance2022 RFC 9113now gRPC-Web for browsers
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): gRPC-Web supports unary and server streaming only, with Envoy as the default proxy.
  • Changed by defaults: MAX_CONNECTION_AGE is infinite by default, so a server must set it to get connections to rebalance.
  • What won't change: a call's outcome is known only at its end, so a trailer or equivalent is needed.

On the wire

Shape only, not a gRPC library: a 64-line stdlib HTTP/2 server on 127.0.0.1 that answers a POST in gRPC's layout (Python 3.15.0). Captured on 1 Nov 2026 with curl 8.7.1:

< HTTP/2 200
< content-type: application/grpc
< grpc-status: 0
< grpc-message: OK

send HEADERS stream=1 flags=0x4         # ③ response headers
send DATA    stream=1 len=10            # ④ 5-byte prefix + "hello"
send HEADERS stream=1 flags=0x5         # ⑤ trailers + END_STREAM

curl prints the trailers with the headers, but the frame log shows they came after the body. flags=0x5 is END_HEADERS plus END_STREAM, which is the trailer signature. A 200 here says nothing about the call's success, which is why logs that record only HTTP status report every failed RPC as healthy.

Measure it

  • See it: grpcurl -v prints status and trailers per call, illustrative here; curl --http2 -v showed the same trailers above.
  • In production: per method, grpc-status counts; per backend, calls per second; per connection, age and active streams.
  • Bounded by: pinned connections → L7 balancing, or MAX_CONNECTION_AGE with _GRACE; stuck calls → a grpc-timeout deadline on every call.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: gRPC puts one call on one HTTP/2 stream, with a 5-byte prefix per message, and it reports the result in trailers at the end of the stream. So it depends on HTTP/2's streams, cancel, flow control and trailers. Browsers can't read raw trailers, so they need gRPC-Web. And because a long connection carries many calls, balancing must happen per call.

Q · Mechanism — Why does gRPC return HTTP 200 for a failed call? Because the HTTP status is sent before the outcome is known. A streaming call may fail after a thousand messages, so the status has to come at the end. The HTTP status says the transport delivered a response; grpc-status in the trailer says what happened. Metrics built on HTTP status therefore miss every application error.

Q · Trade-off — Is gRPC worth requiring HTTP/2 end to end? Inside a service mesh, usually: streams, deadlines, cancel and a typed contract pay for themselves. At a public edge, less so: browsers need a translation proxy, and any intermediary must pass trailers. If callers are mostly browsers or partners, the API choice framework often lands on REST, with gRPC behind the edge.

Compare

Need HTTP/2 feature Why HTTP/1.1 falls short When you'd care
Concurrent calls streams one response at a time any fan-out
Status after body trailing HEADERS needs chunked, patchy support streaming RPC
Cancel one call RST_STREAM closes the connection deadlines
Backpressure per call stream windows connection only server streaming

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Message prefix 5 bytes 1 flag + 4 length spec: gRPC PROTOCOL-HTTP2
Stream per call 1 always spec: gRPC PROTOCOL-HTTP2
MAX_CONNECTION_AGE infinite servers must set it default (as of Nov 2026): gRPC keepalive guide
Frames, unary response 3 HEADERS, DATA, HEADERS measured: curl 8.7.1, 1 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "A 200 means the call worked"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: that's what 200 means everywhere else.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: gRPC's result is grpc-status in the trailer. Application errors arrive inside a 200.
    ↳ Think instead: read the trailer; alert on grpc-status, not HTTP status.
  • "gRPC can fall back to HTTP/1.1"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: most HTTP clients fall back without being told.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the protocol assumes concurrent streams, per-stream cancel and trailers. There's no such mode in PROTOCOL-HTTP2.
    ↳ Think instead: no HTTP/2, no gRPC. A translating proxy is the only bridge.
  • Not the same: RST_STREAM vs GOAWAY
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both stop work on a connection.
    ↳ Difference: RST_STREAM ends one call. GOAWAY tells the peer to stop opening streams, so a drain lets calls finish.
    ↳ Think instead: one cancels a call; the other drains a connection.
  • Don't put gRPC behind an L4 balancer without connection age limits.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's already deployed, and calls succeed.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every call stays on the backend it connected to, so scaling out adds idle pods.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler first step: set MAX_CONNECTION_AGE with a grace period, then consider L7.
  • Shelf life: the wire mapping is stable. gRPC-Web's limits and proxy defaults can change, so re-check them.

Connections

Path:when each version mattersgRPC on HTTP/2gRPC
  • Builds on HTTP/2 framing: one call, one stream.
  • Owned elsewhere: gRPC and HTTP/2 balancing owns the L4 problem; gRPC in production owns operations.
  • Composes with gRPC: the contract on top.
  • Sized by the timeout hierarchy: grpc-timeout carries the deadline.
